# Test fixtures

The files in this directory are generated by the backend but committed on purpose: the frontend test
suite must not need a Python environment. With the fixtures in the repository, `npm test` checks
cross-language consistency and the rejection of malformed payloads on any machine with Node.js.

| File | Generated by | Regenerate when |
|---|---|---|
| `geometry-vectors.json` | `uv run python scripts/emit-geometry-fixture.py` | Geometry code, phantom definitions or the reslice kernel change |
| `chaos/*.bin` and `chaos/manifest.json` | `uv run python scripts/emit-chaos-fixtures.py` | The wire framing or the fault-injection modes change |

Run both commands from the repository root. Build the reslice kernel first (`./scripts/build-kernel.sh`):
the `kernel` section of `geometry-vectors.json` holds reference outputs computed by the native build. If
the native kernel is not available, the section is marked unavailable and the WebAssembly kernel tests
are skipped.

Commit regenerated fixtures together with the change that caused them. CI regenerates both sets and runs
`scripts/check-fixture-sync.py`, which fails when the result differs meaningfully from the committed
version: the JSON is compared structurally with a small floating-point tolerance, and the `.bin` files
must match byte for byte.

## Why one side generates and the other side asserts

If each language had its own tests, passing them would show that each implementation agrees with itself,
not that the implementations agree with each other. What must hold is that Python and the browser compute
the same voxel index for the same world coordinate. So Python computes the answers and TypeScript asserts
them.

The same applies to `chaos/*.bin`: these are malformed frames that the test backend actually produced, not
frames that the frontend built for itself. A frontend that only rejects the bad data it imagines is not
tested against the bad data the backend can send.
